topIssues.title: op-deployer forge package: tests can't pass in any single environment (PATH-dependent)
topIssues.author: ajsutton
topIssues.body:
While auditing which Go packages are missing from the `go-tests` CI list (`TEST_PKGS`), I found `op-deployer/pkg/deployer/forge` has a test suite (7 test funcs) that has **never run in CI** and cannot pass in any single environment.

### Root cause

`StandardBin.Ensure` prefers a `forge` already on `PATH` when its version matches the pinned `StandardVersion`, before ever attempting a download:

```go
// op-deployer/pkg/deployer/forge/binary.go:193
// 2) PATH: use if version matches the pinned Version
if forgePath, err := exec.LookPath("forge"); err == nil {
    if ver, err := getForgeVersion(ctx, forgePath); err == nil && ver == StandardVersion {
        b.path = forgePath
        return nil
    }
}
```

This makes the package's tests mutually exclusive:

- **`forge` on PATH** (the CI/mise environment, which pins forge 1.2.3): `TestStandardBinary_Downloads` fails — `Ensure` short-circuits to the on-PATH binary instead of downloading.
  - `download_OK`: `bin.Path()` returns the mise forge path, not `cacheDir/forge`.
  - `invalid_checksum`: expects a `checksum mismatch` error but gets `nil` (download/checksum is never reached).
- **`forge` absent from PATH**: `TestMinimalSources`, `TestClient_Smoke`, `TestClient_OutputRedirection`, `TestScriptCaller` all fail with `could not find binary: exec: "forge": executable file not found in $PATH`.

### Repro

```
# With forge on PATH (e.g. via mise):
go test -tags=ci ./op-deployer/pkg/deployer/forge/...   # TestStandardBinary_Downloads fails

# Without forge on PATH:
go test -tags=ci ./op-deployer/pkg/deployer/forge/...   # smoke/MinimalSources fail
```

### Suggested fix

Isolate the download-path tests from the host `forge` — e.g. inject the `LookPath` lookup (or set `t.Setenv("PATH", "")`) in `TestStandardBinary_Downloads` so it exercises the download + checksum logic deterministically regardless of whether a matching forge is installed.

Once the package passes reliably, add `./op-deployer/pkg/deployer/forge/...` to `TEST_PKGS`.

Context: follow-up to #21197, which adds the gap packages that *do* pass.

---
*Filed by Claude (AI assistant) on Adrian's behalf.*

topIssues.title: op-deployer: typed intent schema for OP Private settlement groups
topIssues.author: karlfloersch
topIssues.body:
OP Private's `settlementChainId` is an untyped op-deployer deploy override (#23657). A chain sets it to its own ID to be a settlement chain, or to another chain's ID to be a private chain. #23953 builds settlement groups on that override: a private chain reuses its settlement chain's L1 contracts, and `checkSettlementGroups` rejects groups that would deploy inconsistently.

When OP_PRIVATE graduates, replace the override with a typed intent schema for settlement groups:
- a typed `settlementChainId` field instead of the deploy override;
- a separate, smaller config type for private chains that has only the values a private chain really sets (its L2 values, start block, genesis time and so on), and no L1 values such as `l1ProxyAdminOwner`, the other L1 roles, custom gas token or dispute game settings, which come from its settlement chain.

Today a private chain is a full `ChainIntent`, and `checkPrivateChainL1Config` compares each L1 field with the settlement chain's, so every new L1 field needs a new check and is easy to miss (raised in https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/pull/23953#discussion_r4488509183). With a private chain type, those values have nowhere to go, and the checks go away.

Code: `op-deployer/pkg/deployer/pipeline/settlement.go` (`SettlementChainIDOverride`, `checkSettlementGroups`, `checkPrivateChainL1Config`), and the `TODO(#23978)` there.

topIssues.title: [Bug] EIP-1271 signatures bypass the Safe timelock
topIssues.author: maurelian
topIssues.body:
This finding documents an issue in our codebase which is not active in production. 

TimelockGuard only exists inside the SaferSafes singleton at 0xA8447329e52F64AED2bFc9E7a2506F7D369f483a (version 1.10.1, created 1 Dec 2025). That contract has never emitted GuardConfigured or TransactionScheduled. Every Safe that has installed it turned on the liveness module only, with the guard slot left empty and timelockDelay at 0.

## Description

TimelockGuard is meant to stop a phished or otherwise compromised quorum of signers from acting immediately. Its NatSpec states that cancellation can stop a single phished set of signatures entirely and names module transactions as the only path that the delay does not cover. The guard enforces the delay only in checkTransaction(), which the Safe calls from its own execTransaction(). checkAfterExecution() is empty. configureTimelockGuard() checks the Safe version and the delay but never inspects the fallback handler of the Safe.

A Safe can exercise its authority without calling execTransaction(). When it owns another Safe, that child Safe accepts a contract signature (v == 0) by calling isValidSignature(data, signature) on the owner. The guarded Safe has no such function, so the call reaches its fallback handler. The default CompatibilityFallbackHandler wraps the data in a SafeMessage hash and calls checkSignatures() against the owners of the guarded Safe. No transaction of the guarded Safe exists at any point. Nothing is scheduled, nothing appears in pendingTransactions() and cancelTransaction() has no hash to act on.

The OP Stack ownership model relies on such nested Safes. The Guardian Safe has the Security Council Safe as its only owner and a threshold of one. The ProxyAdmin owner is a Safe owned by the Security Council Safe and the Foundation Upgrade Safe. On mainnet, the Security Council Safe already uses CompatibilityFallbackHandler and the Guardian Safe has no guard. Consider a Security Council Safe that is upgraded to Safe 1.4.1 and protected by the guard as documented:

An attacker obtains a quorum of Security Council signatures over the SafeMessage hash of a Guardian Safe transaction that calls swapOwner() to replace the Security Council Safe with the attacker.
Any caller submits that transaction to execTransaction() on the Guardian Safe with a contract signature from the Security Council Safe. The Guardian Safe executes it in the same block.
The attacker becomes the sole owner of the Guardian Safe and holds the Guardian role. It can pause every chain that uses the SuperchainConfig, extend that pause past its expiry, unpause during an incident and call the Guardian functions of the AnchorStateRegistry.
The honest signers have nothing to cancel and the Security Council Safe loses control of the Guardian Safe. Restoring the role requires an upgrade of SuperchainConfig with a new guardian. That upgrade must itself wait for the Security Council timelock. The same path lets phished quorums of both owner Safes execute a ProxyAdmin owner transaction, such as a contract upgrade, without any delay. Consequently, the guard does not protect the authority that the Security Council exercises through other Safes, which is where its protocol powers reside.

# Recommendation

Make configureTimelockGuard() reject a Safe whose fallback handler can validate signatures without a scheduled transaction. Read the handler from the fallback handler storage slot of the Safe and require it to be zero or an approved handler that only honors messages recorded in signedMessages. Apply the same check in checkAfterExecution() so that a scheduled transaction cannot install such a handler later.

topIssues.title: op-deployer: run live bootstrap and apply through netchef's proxyd before the v0.9 RC
topIssues.author: nonsense
topIssues.body:
#23664 moves live `apply` and `bootstrap` onto forge: a keyless run on a fork of the L1 head, then a replay of the recorded transactions through txmgr. Three of its behaviours only show up behind a load-balanced RPC such as proxyd, and CI covers none of them, because CI sends only to anvil:

1. proxyd answers 403 to some methods that forge calls.
2. A read can reach a backend that lags the one that took the send. The next script forks at or after the block of the send.
3. A backend can report a stale pending nonce. op-deployer waits up to 2 min for the deployer's pending transactions.

Also watch one more spot. txmgr reads the nonce once per script with `NonceAt(latest)`, for the script's first transaction. That read comes after op-deployer's own nonce check. A backend that is behind the last send makes the signer refuse (`deployment nonce changed`) and stops `apply`. That fails safe, but it fails the run.

## Run

op-deployer from develop or the RC, against Sepolia through the proxyd L1 endpoint that netchef uses, with a throwaway funded key:

- `bootstrap superchain`
- `bootstrap implementations`
- `init` and `apply --deployment-target live` for one chain with additional dispute games
- `apply` again, which should send nothing

## Pass

- Every step completes, with no `deployment nonce changed` or `nonce mismatch`.
- Fork reruns (`forge run on the L1 fork failed; running it again`) and waits (`waiting for the L1 head`, `waiting for the deployer's pending transactions`) are rare and short.
- No 403 or 429 on a method that op-deployer needs.

This blocks the v0.9 op-deployer release candidate, before netchef picks it up.

Context: https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/pull/23664#issuecomment-6684159918

topPRs.title: ci: pilot RWX with shared routing and shadow tests
topPRs.author: teddyknox
topPRs.body:
PR validation currently rebuilds op-reth in CircleCI and lacks executed RWX parity evidence. This pilot runs the complete op-reth release producer and its three associated checks alongside shared routing, Go lint/Rust formatting, Go rollup tests and four standard-contract configurations. CircleCI continues to own the required gates.

The op-reth shadow builds both release binaries, runs every selected `reth-optimism-node` test through a nextest archive, generates fresh compact vectors with pinned develop and reads them with the PR binary, and regenerates both superchain snapshots. It uses shared dependency downloads, content caching, separate native tool caches for Cargo targets and sccache, parallel codec compilers, pinned tools and SHA-bound artifacts. Checksum-matching superchain bundles retain their timestamps. Release, integration and codec consumers mount artifacts directly instead of inheriting compiler-cache layers. Every verdict and vector generation executes freshly.

Validation:

- At `0b7935e7339726c1b1166be6372fbf057fb251dd`, [native op-reth CI](https://cloud.rwx.com/optimism/runs/0d4989f8fc044b48888ba7cdda9e9b2a) passed all four workloads in **6m20s**. All 50 runnable integration cases passed; one explicitly ignored case remained in discovery. Original JUnit identities and outcomes matched [CircleCI job 5625881](https://circleci.com/gh/ethereum-optimism/optimism/5625881) exactly. All four RWX status checks are green at this head.
- Direct artifact mounts removed both compiler-cache trees from the codec verifier. Its measured preparation fell from 171s at `99ccc76a` to 2s at this head, followed by fresh execution in 5s. The final consumer received a 622 MiB binary artifact and two small vector/provenance artifacts, and its metadata confirmed the PR checkout. Both observations are single samples, with different runner-local layer states.
- Before the bundle/artifact optimizations, the complete RWX run at `d2b90241` took 13m10s initially and [5m58s with warm tool caches](https://cloud.rwx.com/optimism/runs/2c7e09f8233541869ff6fa8771b3d372). A [forced target-cache probe](https://cloud.rwx.com/optimism/runs/8545eb684d094e13abc4e91fdab645fe) after bundle retention executed snapshot preparation in 7s, with six Rust sccache hits and zero misses; fresh regeneration still ran for 24s.
- An [empty-target probe](https://cloud.rwx.com/optimism/runs/8552f40db3314cf282583313806e0be6) produced 263 Rust hits and zero misses in 36s. An [identical-input release rerun](https://cloud.rwx.com/optimism/runs/be0b0006cd5044c88739ec46cd81f2d6) reused the compiler content cache and finished the release path in 8s, including fresh binary verification. A separate warm release rebuild recorded 27 Rust hits and no misses but still spent 236s compiling/linking; content reuse and incremental reuse have different benefits.
- An [intentional CLI-only test fault](https://cloud.rwx.com/optimism/runs/add6576e7432497a8a1e3f85a40a8313) failed the task and run, preserved nextest's exit 100, and retained original JUnit and partial coverage. Committed Rust tests were unchanged.
- 22 cache/provenance/report regression tests, 35 routing scenarios, shell checks and RWX configuration validation passed. The final native artifact consumers inherited no op-reth compiler caches; only snapshot regeneration retained Cargo targets.

Implementation coverage is **10/86 expanded PR jobs, about 12%**. The [parity checklist](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/codex/rwx-ci-pilot/docs/ai/rwx-parity-todos.md) and [measurements](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/codex/rwx-ci-pilot/docs/ai/rwx-migration.md#first-hosted-measurements) track representative Rust source-change probes, repeated actual-resource timings and billed usage, smaller tool/compiler layers, and a protected cache-rebuild policy before promotion. Whole-run duration, compiler phases and billed cost remain separate measurements; declared resource classes do not prove identical hardware. Full Go/acceptance producers and consumers, remaining Rust/contracts, routing and identity cutover remain open.

Earlier Go/contract comparisons at `587b4c3a` still need authoritative CircleCI discovery, 178 contract skip reasons and fresh evidence for 17 cached Go cases. Schedules, publishing and privileged writer ownership remain with CircleCI. The cache-only RWX vault has no production credentials and restricted pilot/develop writers; remove the temporary pilot grant and evict pilot cache entries before promotion.

This single draft PR replaces #23141, #23142, #23144 and #23148 and remains the ongoing home for the pilot.

topPRs.title: op-deployer: add a hidden receipt poll interval and use 50ms in integration tests
topPRs.author: mds1
topPRs.body:
**Metrics** (`go-tests`, 4 runs against 8 merge-queue runs)
- Slowest node: 678s -> about 264s (-61%)
- Job: 762s -> about 328s (-57%)
- Compute: about 2200 -> about 1380 node-seconds (-37%)
- Merge queue entry, modeled from 24 recent entries: median about 1300s -> about 1207s (-7%). `go-tests` is the most common long pole after #23974.

**Problem**

Since #21728 the keyed broadcaster sends one transaction at a time and waits for its receipt. txmgr checks on a ticker, 1s by default, so each transaction costs at least 1s even though Anvil mines on send. That was about 37s of each 42s `TestEndToEndContinuePreparedChain` case.

**Change**

Integration tests now poll every 50ms. The apply tests already could, so this passes the interval through bootstrap and continue, and adds a hidden `--receipt-query-interval` flag for the CLI tests.

**Why the diff is bigger than the speedup**

The speedup is about 80 of the 323 changed lines (`git diff -w`). The rest stops a new poll setting from harming a real deployment:
- **Limits of 50ms-1s, or 0 for the default, checked first on all four commands.** Slow polling can miss a mined transaction's receipt until rebroadcasts abort the send, at about 36s or more. Fast polling adds RPC load, because each rebroadcast of a stuck transaction adds a poller: at 50ms, about 100 requests a second after a minute, against about 5 at 1s.
- **A warning on any interval other than 1s.** A stray `DEPLOYER_RECEIPT_QUERY_INTERVAL` can't apply silently. The warning and the hidden flag mark this as test-only, since fast polling also makes a load-balanced RPC likelier to serve the next gas estimate from a lagging replica.
- **About 220 lines of tests.** They fail if an unset interval polls faster than 1s, if the limits move, or if a command stops passing the interval on. Otherwise a wrong default would reach every real deployment with CI still green.

With the flag unset, a deployment behaves as before: same 1s poll, same tx manager settings, no warning and no new error path.

**Tradeoffs**
- `NewKeyedBroadcaster` now rejects intervals outside the limits. No caller in this repo sets one, but an out-of-tree caller passing 2s would get an error.
- sysgo's existing 100ms logs one warning per devstack.

topPRs.title: ci: gate proposal/** branches with a ci-gate-proposals workflow
topPRs.author: maurelian
topPRs.body:
Me: Define a subset of CI workflows that are required on proposal branches. Since  only op-contracts and op-deployer are released from those branches, we only care about workflows affecting them.

Claude: 

Release branches (`proposal/**`) run the full develop CI and rot within weeks of being cut: Rust toolchain drift, new RUSTSEC advisories and a Codecov uploader that none of the branch's own changes touch. A patch release then starts with days of unrelated fix-ups, which is why we did not ship an `op-deployer/0.7.x` patch in August. Context and plan: [P/PS: Release Branch CI Maintainability](https://app.notion.com/p/oplabs/P-PS-Release-Branch-CI-Maintainability-3c6f153ee16280958a4fcb71400aa658).

After this change, a proposal branch, a PR into it, its merge queue and an API trigger on it run one workflow, `release-branch`, and are gated by its one check, `ci-gate-proposals`: the contracts jobs that `required-contracts-ci` gates on develop, the NUT and op-deployer forge-version checks, and `go-tests`. Nothing changes for `develop` or feature PRs into it. A PR is routed by its base, so a PR from a proposal branch into develop still gets the develop gates.

Two things a reviewer cannot see in the diff:

- **The proposal/\*\* GitHub ruleset must require `ci-gate-proposals` before this config reaches a release branch.** On a proposal branch none of the four develop gates are produced, so a ruleset that still requires them blocks every PR rather than passing it unverified. Today `enforce-ci-checks-develop` covers `proposal/op-contracts/v7.*` and `v8.*`. This PR only lands the config on `develop`; the ruleset change and the cherry-pick onto v8.0.0 and v9.0.0 are separate steps.
- **A branch pushed before its PR exists is routed as a develop PR**, since there is no base yet. A push after the PR is opened re-routes it. The usual `git push` then `gh pr create` flow against a release branch therefore needs one more push.

Dismissed from the CI config review: keeping the whole `go-tests` job rather than splitting op-deployer's tests out. We want to see whether the Go suite rots on a release branch before paying for a split.

A PR into `develop` never takes the new routing, so this PR's own checks do not exercise the workflow. The same commits are pushed to a throwaway [`proposal/ci-test`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/tree/proposal/ci-test) branch, where the routing takes the release-branch path and `ci-gate-proposals` is the only gate: [CI runs on that branch](https://app.circleci.com/pipelines/github/ethereum-optimism/optimism?branch=proposal%2Fci-test). The runs at [f1d8917](https://app.circleci.com/workflow/636ff79d-a051-48b0-90e4-ece304c1d92c), [897f167](https://app.circleci.com/workflow/205a6488-9419-4009-8edc-629c44b89f80) and [4db2ed9](https://app.circleci.com/workflow/d7da5e50-de1a-4951-b2bc-91696d33683a) (the current head) all passed.

topPRs.title: op-acceptance-tests: run each test in its own go test
topPRs.author: mds1
topPRs.body:
**Metrics** (memory-all, kona / op-node)
- Slowest node: 1154s / 1100s -> about 400s / 400s (-65%)
- Job: about 1250s -> about 480s (-60%)
- Mean node: about 660s -> about 350s (-47% compute)
- Merge queue entry, modeled from 24 recent entries: median 1809s -> about 1300s (-28%). memory-all is the long pole today. After this, `go-tests` is the most common one, then `kona-proof-action-single`.
- Highest peak memory on any node: 35.5 GiB -> 32.4 GiB (2 runs each)

**Problem**

Each acceptance job splits its tests across 8 nodes, and each node runs `go test -p 8 -parallel 1`. That allows 8 packages at once, but only one test at a time within a package. Heavy packages like `proofs/zk` run their tests one after another, so one node can take about 1150s while the average is about 660s, and the job waits for its slowest node. Nodes also sit partly idle, averaging about 4 tests at once despite a cap of 8.

**Changes**
- Each top-level test gets its own `go test`, up to `ACCEPTANCE_TEST_JOBS` at once, using `xargs -P` as `rust/kona/tests/justfile` does. I rejected a custom scheduler: it was just as fast at about 730 more lines.
- A test name shared by several packages goes to one node, which runs every package's copy once. `TestOperatorFee` ran 9 times and now runs 3.
- 14 parent tests run their subtests serially. Go stops a parent's clock during parallel subtests, so they recorded about 0s and the splitter piled them onto one node. CI already ran these subtests one at a time.
- `TestInteropFaultProofs_IntraBlock` (485s) becomes 7 top-level tests, with the same case bodies. `-run .../CascadeInvalid` no longer selects a case; use the new test name.
- `-timeout` stays 30m but is now per test. The longest test takes about 381s. The default `ACCEPTANCE_TEST_JOBS` goes from 12 to the 8 CI runs. Results and JSON logs are one file per test.

**Why it's safe**
- Same 884 test rows per job, each exactly once, same results (863 passed + 21 skipped, 873 + 11).
- Still at most 8 tests per node, checked from test event timestamps.
- Planted bad tests on CI (fail, panic, background panic, SIGKILL, exit 255, exit 0) fail the job and leave the real tests' results unchanged.
- A test must start and report a pass or skip, so a stale name or a `TestMain` that swallows a failure now fails the job. So do unexpected `go test -list` output, an empty shard and a test that never ran. A crash no longer loses the rest of its package's results.
- Two tests from one package can now overlap. I found no shared on-disk paths, fixed ports, `TestMain` or mutable package state they rely on. That's a code audit plus 28 clean job runs, not a proof under load.

**Tradeoffs**
- Nodes now stay near 8 tests instead of about 4, which could make load-related flakes more likely.
- As today, a test killed by a timeout can leave its devstack running until the job ends. With 30m per test, a node where everything hangs could take about 135m.
- The first queue entries after merge may see about 600s, until `develop` has fresh test timings.
- Console output can tear when several tests fail at once. `failed/`, `per-test/` and JUnit aren't affected.
- `TestMain` and `init` can no longer print to stdout, because stray `go test -list` output fails the job.

**Dismissed review findings**
- A test that prints a fake pass line and then calls `syscall.Exit(0)` still passes. It would have to be deliberate.
- A `TestMain` that exits 0 during `-list` hides its package, as it does in CI today. There's no `TestMain` in the tree, and a guard would fail on helper-only packages.
- A new IntraBlock case needs a matching test, and nothing enforces it. The alternatives parse test names.
- Nodes don't check that the split covers every test across nodes, as today.
- `TestChainFork` keeps one parallel subtest. The effect on its recorded time is small.
- `run_test` stays in the justfile rather than a new script, matching kona's.
